summary: Hono is an HTTP framework built on Web Standards. A small core in src (hono.ts, context.ts, compose.ts) sits behind four interchangeable router implementations, a large catalogue of opt-in middleware, and one adapter per runtime, so the same app runs on Bun, Deno, workerd, Lambda and Node.

districts.name: The Foundry
districts.purpose: The framework itself: the app class, the request context, middleware composition, the routers, the JSX renderer and the runtime adapters.

districts.name: Proving Grounds
districts.purpose: Integration suites that boot the framework on each supported runtime instead of mocking it.

districts.name: Speed Trials
districts.purpose: Standalone packages that time the routers, JSX rendering and query parsing against other frameworks.

districts.name: Instrument Yard
districts.purpose: Bundle size and type-check budgets recorded on every run so performance regressions show up as numbers.

districts.name: The Works
districts.purpose: The release pipeline: it builds the many published entry points and validates them before they ship.

districts.name: Knowledge District
districts.purpose: Contribution rules, the code of conduct and the migration guide; the user manual lives on a separate site.

districts.name: Civic Offices
districts.purpose: Five workflows covering continuous integration, autofix, code review, stale issues and releases.

importantModules.role: The Hono application class, assembled from hono-base and the default router; this is what an app imports first.
The Context object handed to every handler: request access, response helpers and per-request state.
Builds the onion-shaped middleware chain that wraps each matched handler.
The Router interface every routing implementation satisfies; the seam that makes routing swappable.
Picks between the other routers at first request by trying them and keeping the one that fits the route set.
Compiles all routes into one regular expression for constant-time matching; the fastest of the four.
Trie-based router used when routes are too dynamic for the regexp router to pre-compile.
One folder per platform (Bun, Deno, Cloudflare, Lambda, Netlify, Vercel, service worker), each a separate published entry point.
The opt-in middleware catalogue: auth, CORS, CSRF, caching, compression, ETag, JWT, logging and more.
The typed RPC client that mirrors a server's route types back to the caller.
The built-in JSX runtime used for server rendering and, through src/jsx/dom, on the client.

strengths: The core is genuinely small: hono.ts, context.ts and compose.ts carry the framework and everything else is opt-in.
Routing is pluggable behind one Router interface, with four implementations and a smart router that chooses between them.
Runtime support is isolated in src/adapter, so a new platform is a new folder rather than a change to the core.
Tests sit beside the code as src/*.test.ts, and runtime-tests additionally boots the framework on Deno, Bun, Node, workerd, Fastly and Lambda.
Bundle size and type-check cost are measured in perf-measures on an ongoing basis, not just at release time.
concerns: The middleware catalogue and the adapters live in the same repository as the core, so the published surface is wide and every release moves all of it.
Almost the whole codebase sits under one src directory; the meaningful structure is a level deeper, which makes the top level look flatter than the project is.
The user-facing documentation lives on a separate site, so this repository's docs folder only covers contribution and migration.
